traits.height_max_m.note: FEIS review (Fryer 2021), Botanical Description: Himalayan blackberry stands in western Oregon were 0.8 m to 3.4 m tall, mean 1.5 m; its arching canes are generally 1 m to 7 m long. No old flora covers the species: Abrams, Jepson 1925, Sargent and Silvics lack it.

traits.juvenile_period_years.note: FEIS (Rubus armeniacus, R. bifrons review, read): Himalayan blackberry seedlings take 3 years to produce flowering canes; the Woody Plant Seed Manual's Rubus chapter gives no age.

generator.params.path_half.note: A choice of the model's (crown form step B, broadleaf revision 11): the wood from the base at which a shoot's nodes are half as long, fitted so the plant grows to the height of its oldest reference size, with the crown's width left to grow inside the loose region.

generator.params.note: Hand-set from general knowledge of the species: an invasive bramble of thick, arching, thorny canes that root at the tips and build impenetrable mounds, with leaves of five toothed leaflets and pale pink flowers. Not fitted to measurements.

allometry.note: Rough sizes from general knowledge of the species: 2.3 m tall at 12 years in the open. Replace with measured data before calling this species calibrated.

appearance.note: Colours chosen by eye: dark green leaflets, pale beneath; pale pink flowers; red-purple canes. Fruit (plant roadmap P4), as in mid-July: panicles of berries, most still green or red, the first black. Its year (appearance.organs.bloom.season) is authored from general knowledge of the species in the south Puget Sound lowlands: white to pink flowers in June and July; berries green, red, then black from August into October. The forest's packages show day 196 (mid-July) until the phenology of plant roadmap P5 sets the day from the date and the local climate.

taxon.note: Scientific and common names (and USDA symbol, where given) as the spec's authors wrote them, and the genus the scientific name is written in.

growth_form.note: The growth form the spec's authors chose from the plant's habit.

growth.note: The growth plan (years, step, keyframes) chosen for growing and rendering, not a botanical fact.

variants.note: The environments, conditions and seeds chosen for growing and rendering, not a botanical fact.

taxon.family.note: WCVP v16's family for the accepted name.

taxon.plant_name_id.note: WCVP v16's plant_name_id for the accepted species the name resolves to (the accepted name).

appearance.organs.bloom.season.flower_lo.note: Its flowers drawn one by one (spec rework L1b): white to pale pink flowers 2 to 2.5 cm across with many stamens, drawn opening together. From general descriptions of the species (OregonFlora, the Flora of North America and nursery and extension pages as quoted in search results; the pages themselves were not read). The size is the flower's width, or a closed corolla's length, over the fruit's length, roughly as in life. Its flower laid out whorl by whorl (spec rework P5b): five white or pale pink petals between five sepals on a floral cup, a hundred stamens and thirty free pistils, from the characters of its own, Rosaceae's and Rubus's by the rules at the flowering plants.

traits.note: Oregon State University's Landscape Plants page on the species, as search results quote it (the page itself was not read): leaves alternate, palmately compound, with 3 to 5 obovate to elliptic leaflets, each 4 to 8 cm long, their margins irregularly serrate, grey-green and softly hairy beneath. Five on the first-year canes the model draws. Bugwood and americansouthwest.net, as quoted in search results; the pages themselves were not read: a hundred or more brown-tipped stamens and over 30 pistils; the Flora of North America's genus key gives the floral cup 3 to 10 mm across (as quoted in search results; the page itself was not read). Thirty pistils is the most a flower draws.

appearance.organs.leaf.shape.note: The leaf drawn as a palmately compound leaf (spec rework P4), its leaflets counted, set and shaped from its characters by the rules at the flowering plants and the plants; before, five leaflets stood along a short rachis. By eye from photographs: the outer pair turned back beside the petiole (230 degrees between them) and 0.65 as long as the end leaflet, each leaflet on a short stalk.
